FIELD GUIDE TO URBAN BEEKEEPING

1. Getting started

Urban beekeeping means keeping honey bee colonies on rooftops, balconies and small gardens.
Before buying bees, check local regulations and inform your neighbours.
Beginners should take a short course and shadow an experienced keeper for one season.

1.1 Choosing a hive

The Langstroth hive uses stacked boxes with removable frames and is the most common design.
The top-bar hive is cheaper and gentler on the back, but its combs are harder to move.
Whichever design you choose, buy standard equipment so that parts are interchangeable.

1.2 Selecting a site

Face the entrance towards the south east so the morning sun wakes the colony early.
Provide a windbreak and a shallow water source with landing stones for the bees.
Keep the flight path away from doors and pavements by placing a tall fence or hedge in front.

2. The colony

A healthy colony has one queen, several hundred drones in summer and up to fifty thousand workers.
The queen lays up to two thousand eggs per day in spring.

2.1 Life cycle of the worker bee

A worker develops from egg to adult in twenty-one days.
During her first weeks she cleans cells and nurses larvae, then builds comb, guards the entrance
and finally becomes a forager in the last three weeks of her short life.

2.2 Swarming

In late spring a crowded colony raises new queens and the old queen leaves with half of the workers.
To reduce swarming, add space with an extra box and remove queen cells during weekly inspections.
A captured swarm can be housed in an empty hive with a few frames of foundation.

3. Seasonal work

3.1 Spring build-up

Inspect the hive on the first warm day above twelve degrees.
Check that the queen is laying, that there is stored food, and replace damaged frames.
Feed thin sugar syrup only when natural nectar is scarce.

3.2 Summer honey flow

Add honey supers before the main nectar flow starts.
Harvest when the bees have capped at least eighty percent of the cells on a frame.
Extract honey with a centrifuge, filter it and store it in clean, sealed jars.

3.3 Autumn preparation

Reduce the entrance with a mouse guard to keep rodents out.
Feed thick sugar syrup in early autumn so the colony can store winter reserves.
Treat against varroa mites once the honey supers have been removed.

3.4 Winter care

Do not open the hive when temperatures are low; the bees form a warm cluster around the queen.
Tilt the hive slightly forward so that condensation runs out of the entrance.
Heft the hive on mild days to estimate whether stores are running low.

4. Pests and diseases

4.1 Varroa mites

The varroa mite feeds on bee larvae and spreads viruses, and is the biggest threat to colonies.
Monitor mite levels with a sticky board or an alcohol wash every month in season.
Approved treatments include oxalic acid vapour in winter and formic acid strips in late summer.

4.2 Foulbrood

American foulbrood is a bacterial disease that turns larvae into a brown, ropey mass.
It is notifiable by law and infected colonies usually have to be burned.
Sunken, perforated cell cappings are an early warning sign.

4.3 Wasps and hornets

Reduce the entrance in late summer when wasps rob weak colonies.
Traps placed away from the apiary can catch queen wasps in spring.
